Use these only with `--mode full`. The build warns if they appear in a baseline page.

**The rule:** an interaction earns its place only if it makes the reader *think
about the idea*: guess, decide, change one thing and watch, or put things in
order. Research is clear that clicking for its own sake adds effort and no
learning, while guessing before seeing the answer reliably improves memory, even
when the guess is wrong.

**How many:** at most one per section on "How it works", and three to six on the
whole page. Full mode turns the explanation up, not the noise.

| Component | Use it when | Counts as the section's quick check |
|---|---|---|
| Guess first (`x-predict`) | the answer surprises people, or a common belief is wrong | yes |
| What if (`x-whatif`) | one variable changes the outcome (amount, distance, size, setting) | no |
| Put it in order (`x-order`) | the section taught a sequence | yes |
| Explore (`x-explore`) | a diagram has 3 to 6 parts, each with its own detail | no |
| Scroll story (`x-scrolly`) | one diagram changes through 3 to 6 stages as the text explains them | no |
| Exploded view (`x-exploded`) | a system is made of stacked layers | no |
| Zoomable map (`x-zoom`) | the reader needs the big picture, then the detail of each part | no |
| Read aloud | automatic in full mode: a **Listen** button in the top bar, and a voice button on every walkthrough | n/a |

Wrap interactions in `x-card`. Start a quick-check card with an `x-head` line:
`<div class="x-head"><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-list-ordered"/></svg>Quick check · put it in order</div>`.

## Guess first, then see

```html
<div class="x-card x-predict">
  <div class="x-head"><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-message-circle-question"/></svg>Quick check · guess first</div>
  <p class="x-q">A question people usually get wrong?</p>
  <div class="x-choices">
    <button class="x-choice" type="button" aria-pressed="false">A common belief</button>
    <button class="x-choice" type="button" aria-pressed="false" data-correct>The right answer</button>
    <button class="x-choice" type="button" aria-pressed="false">Another option</button>
  </div>
  <div class="x-reveal" hidden>
    <p class="if-right" hidden><b>Right.</b> Why, in a sentence or two.</p>
    <p class="if-wrong" hidden><b>Most people think that.</b> What's actually true, and why.</p>
    <!-- optional: a small diagram that animates in, e.g. a .d-bars or .d-scale -->
  </div>
</div>
```

Write three or four plausible choices, with the common misconception among them.
The wrong-answer text corrects without scolding and gives the reason. Place it
**before** the explanation when you want the guess to prime the reader, or after
it as a check.

## What if…?

```html
<div class="x-card x-whatif" data-labels="Small|Medium|Large|Huge">
  <label for="size">Order size <output></output></label>
  <input id="size" type="range" min="1" max="4" value="1">
  <div class="ui-list">
    <span class="x-fade" data-on="1-">Fits in a bag</span>
    <span class="x-fade" data-on="2-">Needs a box</span>
    <span class="x-fade risky" data-on="4-">Needs a van</span>
  </div>
  <p class="x-result"><span class="ok" data-show="1-3">Same-day delivery.</span><span class="warn" data-show="4-">Next-day only.</span></p>
</div>
```

The slider's value drives `data-show`, `data-on` and `data-at` inside the card,
exactly as steps do in a walkthrough (showme.md). `data-labels` names each value
for the `<output>`, in order from `min`. `x-fade` dims items until they're `on`;
`risky` turns red when on. For continuous visuals, the card also gets `--v` (the
slider's value), which custom CSS can use, for example `width: calc(var(--v) * 25%)`.
Keep it to one slider: one variable, a clear outcome.

## Put it in order

```html
<div class="x-card x-order">
  <div class="x-head"><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-list-ordered"/></svg>Quick check · put it in order</div>
  <p class="x-q">Tap the steps in the order they happen.</p>
  <ol>
    <li><button type="button" data-pos="3"><span>Third step</span></button></li>
    <li><button type="button" data-pos="1"><span>First step</span></button></li>
    <li><button type="button" data-pos="2"><span>Second step</span></button></li>
  </ol>
  <div class="x-row"><button class="x-btn" type="button" data-check>Check</button><button class="x-btn ghost" type="button" data-reset>Start over</button><span class="x-msg" aria-live="polite"></span></div>
</div>
```

`data-pos` is each step's correct place, counting from 1. List them shuffled, and
never in the right order. Tapping a numbered step undoes it and every step after
it. Use four to six steps, with short labels.

## Explore the parts

```html
<div class="x-card x-explore">
  <div class="x-parts">
    <button class="x-part" type="button" data-k="kitchen"><span class="disc"><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-flame"/></svg></span>Kitchen</button>
    <button class="x-part" type="button" data-k="till"><span class="disc"><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-coins"/></svg></span>Till</button>
  </div>
  <div class="x-panel" data-k="kitchen"><p>What it does.</p>
    <div class="x-tags"><span>Knows</span><span class="x-tag"><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-key-round"/></svg>the order</span></div>
    <div class="x-tags"><span>Never sees</span><span class="x-tag no"><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-lock"/></svg>card details</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="x-panel" data-k="till"><p>…</p></div>
</div>
```

The first part opens by default. Any element with `data-k` (not just `.x-part`)
selects the panel with the same `data-k`, so the parts of a diagram can be the
buttons too. Each panel holds a sentence and, if useful, tag rows.

## Scroll story

```html
<section class="section wide">
  <div class="text"><p class="kicker">2.4</p><h2>A question?</h2><p>Scroll through it.</p></div>
  <div class="x-scrolly">
    <div class="scrolly-steps">
      <div class="scrolly-step"><div><b>First</b>, what happens…</div></div>
      <div class="scrolly-step"><div><b>Then</b>…</div></div>
      <div class="scrolly-step"><div><b>Finally</b>…</div></div>
    </div>
    <div class="scrolly-stage">
      <figure class="fig">…a diagram whose parts carry data-show / data-on / data-at…</figure>
    </div>
  </div>
  …quick check…
</section>
```

The diagram stays pinned while the text scrolls past; the step in the middle of
the screen drives it (steps count from 0). A sequence with `data-at` on its rows
works well, as does a flow with `data-on` on its steps. On a phone the diagram
pins to the top.

## Exploded view

```html
<div class="x-card x-exploded">
  <div class="xe-stage"><div class="xe-stack">
    <div class="xe-layer">Top layer</div>
    <div class="xe-layer">Middle layer</div>
    <div class="xe-layer">Bottom layer</div>
  </div></div>
  <div>
    <ol class="xe-list">
      <li><button type="button"><b>Top layer</b><span>What it does, in a sentence.</span></button></li>
      <li><button type="button"><b>Middle layer</b><span>…</span></button></li>
      <li><button type="button"><b>Bottom layer</b><span>…</span></button></li>
    </ol>
    <div class="x-row" style="margin-top:12px"><button class="x-btn ghost" type="button" data-explode>Take it apart</button></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

The stack separates into tilted, numbered plates when it comes into view. Pointing
at or clicking a list item lights its plate, and the button puts the stack back
together. List layers top to bottom, three to seven of them, in the same order in
both places.

## Zoomable map

```html
<div class="x-card x-zoom">
  <div class="xz-view"><div class="xz-world">
    <button class="xz-region" type="button" style="--x:4;--y:10;--w:28;--h:36">
      <b><svg class="ic sm"><use href="#i-globe"/></svg>Part name</b><small>short role</small>
      <span class="xz-detail">Two or three sentences shown when zoomed in.</span>
    </button>
    …more regions…
  </div></div>
  <div class="xz-bar"><span class="xz-where"></span><button class="x-btn ghost" type="button" data-zoom-out>Back to overview</button></div>
</div>
```

`--x`, `--y`, `--w` and `--h` place each region as percentages of the map
(16:10). Lay regions out the way people picture the system: users on the left,
data on the right or bottom. Leave gaps between them. Clicking a region zooms in
until it fills the view and shows its detail; clicking it again, or the button,
zooms out. Use four to eight regions.

## Read aloud

Nothing to write. In full mode the template adds a **Listen** button that reads the
visible page with the browser's own voice, highlighting each block and scrolling
along. Every walkthrough also gets a voice button that narrates each step and waits
for it to finish. Spoken words beside a moving picture teach better than printed
words, because the eyes can stay on the picture. Write the step texts so they make
sense read aloud: no "see left" or "click here".
